claims.text: In equiatomic high-entropy alloys, superconducting behavior is governed by the degree of lattice distortion induced by random chemical mixing.
Lattice distortion modulates electron–phonon coupling strength.
An optimal intermediate level of lattice distortion enhances the pairing potential and raises Tc.
Too little lattice distortion produces insufficient electron–phonon coupling and lower Tc.
Excessive lattice distortion increases electron scattering, which suppresses superconductivity.
Controlled thermal treatments, such as changing annealing temperature or cooling rate, can systematically vary lattice distortion.
Slight compositional tuning can modulate local chemical disorder and lattice distortion.
Chemical disorder produces lattice distortion and local variations in electronic density.
The random distribution of constituent elements creates intrinsic lattice distortions.
Intrinsic lattice distortions alter phonon spectra and electron–phonon coupling constants.
At intermediate distortion, enhanced electron–phonon interaction favors Cooper-pair formation.
At high distortion, enhanced electron scattering acts as a pair breaker.
Tc should have a dome-like dependence on the extent of lattice distortion.
Samples with intermediate lattice distortion should have higher Tc than both more ordered and excessively disordered variants.
A locally ordered, minimally distorted baseline alloy should have lower Tc because it lacks distortion-induced enhancement of electron–phonon coupling.

The proposed relationship is restricted to equiatomic or near-equiatomic alloys having a dominant single solid-solution phase, no significant magnetic impurities or competing phases, and electron–phonon-mediated pairing.
XRD peak broadening and TEM can be used to assess the degree of lattice distortion.
Resistivity and magnetic-susceptibility or magnetization measurements can determine and confirm Tc.
